questions.q: According to this lesson, what are the five real factors in choosing a cloud provider for a given workload?
options: Which provider has the more memorable logo and marketing campaign
Whichever provider a competitor happens to be using
Existing team expertise, specific service capabilities, compliance/data residency, cost, and vendor lock-in
Only the sticker price of compute, ignoring every other factor
questions.explain: These are the honest, defensible factors the lesson walks through — not brand preference.

questions.q: Why does the lesson treat 'the platform your team already knows' as a legitimate factor rather than a cop-out?
options: Ramp-up time, mistakes made while learning, and slower incident response on an unfamiliar platform all have a real dollar cost
Because every cloud provider has identical consoles and tooling, so skill never transfers
Because switching platforms is technically impossible once a team learns one
Because team preference should always override every other business factor automatically
questions.explain: Existing expertise is a real cost factor with measurable consequences, not laziness.

questions.q: In the worked example, why does an acquired startup's existing AWS-specific analytics pipeline become a genuine reason to run multi-cloud?
options: AWS is categorically faster than Azure for every type of workload
Rebuilding it on the acquiring company's existing platform isn't worth the cost, so the inherited AWS pipeline stays in place alongside Azure
Multi-cloud is required by law whenever a company completes an acquisition
The acquired startup's pipeline must be deleted and never referenced again
questions.explain: Inherited infrastructure from a merger or acquisition is one of the lesson's real, honest multi-cloud reasons.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT listed in this lesson as a legitimate reason for genuine multi-cloud use?
options: Inherited infrastructure from a merger or acquisition
"Because we can" — using two providers simply to prove it's technically possible
Redundancy across providers for a workload where an outage is unacceptable
Best-of-breed — picking the single strongest service for a specific job, even across providers
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly says multi-cloud has to earn its place through real operational need, not novelty.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what does 'vendor lock-in' mean as a decision factor?
options: A feature that prevents a provider from ever changing its pricing
A legal requirement that forces a company to use only one cloud provider forever
The amount of storage a provider physically locks behind a paywall
How difficult and costly it would be to migrate a workload away from a given provider later
questions.explain: Vendor lock-in is about future migration difficulty, and the lesson notes some teams accept it deliberately for deeper integration.
